catalog_quote: SYLLABLE STRENGTH LONG VOWELS These are naturally strong and should be lingered upon: (aa) (ii) (oo) (ah) (eh) (ih) (oh) SHORT VOWELS These may be strong if the syllable is formed by a short vowel between two consonants. (closed syllable) ... TWO SYLLABLE WORDS: If the first syllable is strong it is accented. ... pámbiil = book. ... If the first syllable is weak, it is not accented. ... asún = rock ... MULTIPLE SYLLABLE WORDS (THREE OR MORE): The last syllable never gets the accent. The last strong syllable nearest to the final syllable gets the main accent. Usually this means the 2nd to last syllable gets the accent. wtéehiim = strawberry /wŭ-TÉE-hiim/ wteehíimal = strawberries /wŭ-tee-HÍIM-al/ Long words that contain only short vowels and words with sequences of weak syllables alternate stress as : weak-strong-weak-strong Wulamalúsuw. audit.reasoning: Quote check passes: every fragment of the deciding quotation is verbatim in the held munseedelaware.com pronunciation page. The weakness is the KIND of deciding source (undated online pedagogical grammar, author unnamed on the page) when primary literature exists. However, we already hold O'Meara 1990 (McGill PhD, open, 417 pp.), whose phonology appendix rules R23-R24 (thesis pp.50-51) state exactly the analysis our record encodes: long vowels and closed-syllable short vowels strong (= what counts as heavy: CVV+CVC), final syllable extrametrical in 3+ syllable words, main stress on the penult if strong else the antepenult (= right-edge weight-sensitive, non-dominant), alternating weak/strong in runs of open short-vowel syllables (= the secondary-stress rule rhythm), lexical exceptions in loans/reduplication (= strict false). sources.citation: O'Meara, John D. W. 1990. Delaware Stem Morphology. PhD thesis, McGill University. (already held since 2026-09-13, read now for this compilation; not a new download)
sources.quote: R23: final syllables in words of more than two syllables are extrametrical; any long vowel is metrically strong; any short vowel in a closed syllable is metrically strong; in a sequence of open short-vowel syllables odd-numbered vowels are weak, even-numbered strong; loanword and reduplicated short vowels may be exceptionally strong. R24: in words of more than two syllables the penultimate syllable receives main stress if strong, otherwise the antepenult; in disyllables the last strong vowel is stressed (ex. təmahíikan 'axe', təmahíikanal 'axes', asə́n 'stone', áhteew 'it is there').
sources.locator: Appendix to Ch. I 'Phonology', rules R23 Foot Construction and R24 Main Stress Assignment, thesis pp.50-51 (pp.~65-66)

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Munsee language' (raw wikitext, secondary; reports Goddard 1979 p.21 and Goddard 1982)
sources.quote: All syllables with long vowels strong; short vowel in closed syllable strong; in runs of open short-vowel syllables odd-numbered weak, even-numbered strong (Goddard 1979:21); in words longer than two syllables the final syllable is extrametrical and the last strong syllable preceding it takes main stress (payaxkhí·kan vs né·wake); disyllables: strong penult stressed, else final. Secondary source only; useful as a pointer that the primary locus is Goddard 1979 ch.2 p.21.
